# Breathing is slow combustion (respiration and body heat) (`respiration_metabolism`)

<!-- generated by scripts/build_techtree.py from techtree/core/biology.yaml — do not edit -->

- Category: Life sciences (`biology`)
- Deps: needs oxygen_combustion; helped by blood_circulation, air_pump_vacuum, thermometer_temperature
- Core idea: Animals take the same part of the air that a flame needs, combine it with the carbon and hydrogen of their food, and give back fixed air (carbon dioxide), water and heat. Food is fuel; body heat and muscular work come from burning it, slowly and throughout the body, with the blood carrying the gases between tissues and lungs. Demonstrations: breath blown through clear lime water turns it milky, as does the gas from burning charcoal; compare the carbon dioxide in exhaled air with that in room air; a candle flame cannot establish whether enclosed air is safe to breathe. Practical consequences: crowded closed rooms, ships' holds and mines need fresh air, and a charcoal fire in a closed room kills silently.
- Pitfalls:
  - Galen's view that breathing cools the heart
  - Saying the burning happens in the lungs (Lavoisier's own error); it happens in all tissues
  - Thinking breathed-out air has no oxygen left; it still holds about 16 %
  - Relying on a candle to test air: it warns of fixed air in wells and cellars but not of the poisonous gas from smouldering charcoal
- History: islamic: c. 1242 – Ibn al-Nafis: blood is mixed with air in the lungs; europe: 1660s – Boyle and Hooke: animals die in the air pump; Hooke keeps a dog alive by blowing air through its lungs; 1669 Lower: blood turns bright red by contact with air in the lungs; 1674 Mayow's 'nitro-aerial' part of air; 1750s Black finds fixed air in breath; 1783 Lavoisier and Laplace measure a guinea pig's heat and gas output in an ice calorimeter; 1789–1790 Lavoisier and Seguin: oxygen use rises with work, food and cold; 1837 Magnus finds both gases in blood; 1870s Pflüger places respiration in the tissues; americas: 1890s – Atwater's human calorimeter confirms energy balance for food and work
- Read:
  - Antoine Lavoisier and Pierre-Simon Laplace, Mémoire sur la chaleur (presented 1783)
  - Frederic Lawrence Holmes, Lavoisier and the Chemistry of Life (1985)
